units.translation: O hateful divinity, how you have indeed deceived the Persians in your mind.
O wretched me, what a youth of allies he has destroyed!
Who are you, who indeed address me, wretched as I am, with true words?
Who will save me? Who will come to my aid?
How then is King Xerxes faring?
Is Zeus then weaker than these?
You were then in possession of this delightful disease.
with τοι it coalesces by crasis into τἄρα.
More frequently in Sophocles and Euripides τἄρα [then indeed] and οὔ τἄρα [not then indeed].
Shall I then pray for these things for both me and you?
I myself then am contriving against myself (M has ταρρα, Robortellus τ' ἄρα).
You will then burst a sweet-sharp pomegranate.

The epic and lyric poets did not say ἆρα [whether], but ἡ ῥα [then] or ἦρα [then], which the tragedians also sometimes used, as will be said under the word pa. The particle apa is common among the Attic writers, whose use in questions is very frequent, either alone or combined with οὐ [not], μή [not] and certain other particles.

ἄρα and ἄρα differ: for the one pronounced with circumflex accent is an interrogative conjunction, when in doubt we say “ἆρα τέλος ἕξει τὸ πρᾶγμα;” [will the matter have an end?]; but the one with short accent is inferential: if it is day, it is light; but indeed it is day, therefore it is light.
Does he seem to you to be violent?
Does he rouse you with these reproaches, father? Do you raise your dear head upright?
Does she, being wise, find the path of a good tongue?
Is the city of Athens still unsacked?
Does he hear me from below?
Does Orestes perhaps see the light?
Did the sailor, fleeing to the prow, find from the stern a means of safety?

where it is not interrogative, it can seem to be used for ἄρα [then] for the sake of meter, from which, however, it differs in that it does not have the simple inferential force, but serves for asseveration or exclamation. Nor is this surprising: for so great is the connection and affinity between interrogation and exclamation that exclamation seems to be almost nothing but a certain form of questioning, as Hermann observed in the Preface to Oedipus at Colonus p. XVIII of the second edition, where he collected very many examples of this kind from the scenic poets: others have been brought together by others in the Thesaurus vol. 1, 2 p. 1854 and in the Lexicon Sophocleum p.57.
In such oracles indeed (thus Stanley for ἄρα) one must trust.
But he will pay for the dishonor of his father indeed.
[ἀράν [curse] for Ἄρη [Ares] see under the word Αρης.]
